chapter.title: One Hour to Air
chapter.sub: The chief engineer walked out an hour before the news. The picture tears every few seconds.
chapter.status: **DRAFT** · scripted from the owner's request to continue the story · IDs provisional

items.text: SEASON 4 · EPISODE 1 · DRAFT  Countdown · Maya, Tess and Lena · Level L3 → L4  An hour before the evening news, the chief engineer walks out. The picture tears every few seconds. The only person at the desk has been in master control for six weeks.  ⚑ RV-86: timing simplified. RV-80: the roof belongs to facilities. RV-82: figures illustrative. Most choices run on a clock.

items.title: Sixty Minutes to Air
items.stakes: The 6:00 news, live to the whole valley. A trainee alone at the desk. A chief engineer who walked out an hour ago.
items.reward: The news on air, on time. Tess's trust. A list of fourteen warnings you'll spend the season crossing off.

objectives.text: Find out what Cal already knew
Stay off the roof — and still save CAM 2
Move the gateway to an independent reference
Look closer: two things Cal left behind

items.rumor: Cal didn't just quit. He left something taped where only an operator would look.

items.alt: A station parking lot in drizzle. Lena, the director of engineering, on her phone, headset around her neck, pacing.

bubbles.text: I need you in a broadcast control room. Tonight. Our engineer walked out an hour before air.

items.caption: Kestrel Valley Media: one channel, one radio station, one valley. The 6:00 news is live. It always is.

items.alt: Master control: a dark room, a wall of monitors, a red REFERENCE · SYNC ALARM banner across the top. Tess, 22, alone at the desk, hands up, not touching anything.
items.caption: Tess. Six weeks in master control. Alone.

lines.text: Cal said never touch the reference. Cal's gone. So I haven't touched anything. For forty minutes.
That was the right thing to do.

items.alt: Maya arrives, coat still wet, and stands beside Tess in front of the monitor wall. On it, the CAM 2 tile flickers.

bubbles.text: I'm the person Lena called. What's it doing?
CAM 2 and the program return drop every few seconds. Everything else looks fine. I think.

items.caption: The picture tears every few seconds. That's too regular to be random.

items.prompt: Be honest. Is this my fault? I was the only one here when it started.

options.label: “It started at 4:14 on a roof you've never been on. Let's find out what it is.”

items.text: 🔭 PHYSICS IN MOTION  How bad can a clock be?  The science under this episode’s problem — live.

items.sub: Intermediate · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Maya and Tess beside a board. Drift equals p-p-m times ten to the minus six times t. p-p-m is how far off the clock runs; t is the seconds since it lost its reference. And frames? Drift times f-p-s. You do the arithmetic — tell me where we'll be at six.

bubbles.text: Drift equals p-p-m times ten to the minus six times t. p-p-m is how far off the clock runs; t is the seconds since it lost its reference.
Drift times f-p-s. You do the arithmetic — tell me where we'll be at six.

items.caption: Intermediate: the formula and what every letter means. The arithmetic is yours.

items.text: 📗 FIELD NOTES · INTERMEDIATE  Terms   Holdover   Reference clock   ppm   Formula and variables   ƒ FORMULA · Clock drift  drift = ppm × 10 −6  × t   ppm  frequency error, parts per million  t  elapsed time, s  drift  time error, s     ƒ FORMULA · Drift in frames  frames = drift × fps   drift  time error, s  fps  frames per second

items.alt: The status page of Reference A, the master clock: zero satellites since 16:14; holdover for 56 minutes; estimated drift plus 20 parts per million; outputs all running.
items.caption: It hasn't failed. It's running on its own, and slowly going wrong.

items.prompt: 5:11. The master clock is in holdover, drifting. Forty-nine minutes to air. First move?
items.happening: SYNC ALARM. CAM 2 and the return tear every ~6 s.
items.risk: The 6:00 news, the valley's only local news tonight — and Tess's nerve.
timeout: Tess, alone with the silence, reaches for the reboot button Cal told her never to touch.
Under a clock, the loudest button wins unless someone reads first.

hints.text: Which device fails first, and why that one?
Read before you reboot. Then map what depends on what.

options.label: Reboot Reference A
options.result: Eight minutes to relock — and it can't, without the antenna. Its holdover log is gone.
options.consequence: The one record of when and why it lost the sky, erased. Tess watches you do the thing Cal told her never to do.
options.fail: The clock wasn't broken; it was doing its job without its antenna. A reboot erased the evidence and fixed nothing.

options.label: Switch the whole program to the backup master control
options.result: Same tearing, from a different room.
options.consequence: The backup's clock follows Reference A. Lena wonders why you moved everything.
options.fail: A backup that shares the failing part isn't a fallback.

options.label: Read what the clock and the gateway are telling you — then find what depends on what
options.result: Reference A: holdover since 16:14. The gateway: lock lost every six seconds. The IP cameras: steady.
options.consequence: Tess sees the method: the strict device fails first, and the cause is upstream. You haven't touched anything yet.

options.label: Keep calling Cal
options.result: Voicemail. Voicemail. A text: delivered, not read.
options.consequence: Ten minutes spent on someone who has decided not to be here.
options.fail: Tonight the knowledge has to be found in the room, not in a man who walked out.

items.alt: System View of the station's timing: the satellite antenna shows zero satellites; Reference A in holdover, drifting; Reference B locked to Reference A; the tolerant IP cameras steady; the older video gateway losing lock every six seconds, so CAM 2 tears on program; house reference B, black burst, independent, unused.
items.caption: Tolerant devices follow the drift. The strict one breaks first.

items.alt: The shared engineering inbox on a monitor: an email from Cal at 16:02, subject: I'm done, 14 things. Item three is in capitals: backup ref follows the main, it is not a backup. Tess reads it.
items.caption: Sent at 4:02 p.m. — twelve minutes before the antenna lost the sky.

items.title: A coffee, still warm, and a jacket
items.body: He left his jacket. In the pocket, a folded printout of a regional hub brochure — *Centralized master control for nine stations* — with one sentence circled in pen: *one timing source for all sites.*

lines.text: He sent it to the whole engineering inbox. Fourteen numbered warnings. The first one is from two years ago.

items.title: The backup was never a backup.
items.body: Cal's fourteenth-hour email lists fourteen warnings he'd filed over two years. Number three: Reference B is configured to follow Reference A. When A drifts, B drifts with it. Switching to “the backup” — the obvious fix — would have changed nothing. Somebody knew. Nobody acted.
items.label: Test: reason from the new fact before you read on.

items.alt: Tess turns from the screen to Maya.

bubbles.text: He knew. For two years. And he told everyone. And then he left an hour before air?
Tonight we need what he knew, not why he left. Is there anything else he wrote down?

items.label: **First failure point:** where does the timing go wrong? One reading per stage.
**Learn it now:** sync, genlock and timing references — and why a backup must be independent.

Act II — “What's taped inside the door”

items.alt: Maya on the phone to facilities, looking up at the ceiling.

bubbles.text: The antenna lost the sky at 4:14. I'm not asking anyone to go up tonight. I'm asking you to know.

items.caption: The roof is facilities'. The antenna's cable is facilities'. Maya's job is to tell them — with a time.

lines.text: Nobody goes on that roof tonight. Rain, and it's ours.
Agreed. I just need you to know the antenna lost the sky at 4:14.

items.prompt: 5:28. The antenna can't be fixed tonight. If the gateway can't be steadied, what happens to CAM 2?
items.happening: No sky tonight. Gateway still dropping.
items.risk: The interview about the river — and the director's trust in master control.
timeout: The director builds a plan without master control — and stops asking you.
If you don't offer a fallback, people route around you.

hints.text: What survives even if you're wrong?

options.label: Go up on the roof and look at the cable yourself
options.result: The hatch is locked. Facilities, sharply: “Nobody goes up tonight.”
options.consequence: Five minutes and some trust, gone.
options.fail: The roof and the antenna are facilities'. In rain, at night, it's also a safety call — theirs.

options.label: Plan for the worst: re-block the interview on CAM 1 and CAM 3, CAM 2 dark — and keep hunting for a stable reference
options.result: The director moves the guest's chair ten degrees; two cameras cover it.
options.consequence: The show survives even if the gateway doesn't. Now you can think.

options.label: Put CAM 2 on air anyway and hope the tearing is brief
options.result: It tears twice during the rehearsal read.
options.consequence: Viewers see the picture rip across the anchor's face.
options.fail: Hope isn't a fallback. The pattern said every six seconds.

options.label: Ask the director to cancel the interview
options.result: The water authority's guest drives an hour to be here.
options.consequence: You cut content to save a camera.
options.fail: The fallback costs one camera angle. Cancelling costs the story.

items.alt: Tess opens the back door of rack 4. Taped inside, at eye level, a card in heavy handwriting: IF GPS DIES: GATEWAY → HOUSE REF B (black burst, rack 2) — C.
items.caption: Taped where only an operator would look.

items.teaser: the back of the rack card
items.title: A second line, smaller
items.body: *If you're reading this I'm not here. Tell Lena #3 again.* Dated two years ago, the week warning #3 went unanswered. He knew. He wrote it where you'd find it. Then he waited for someone to read it.

items.title: He wrote the fix where your eyes land.
items.body: The card is dated the same week as warning #3. Cal knew the backup followed the main — so he wrote down the one reference in the building that doesn't: house black in rack 2, independent of the sky. Nobody had opened rack 4's door in two years.
items.label: Test: before Tess changes anything, what should she say out loud?

items.alt: System View after the change: the video gateway's reference now comes from house reference B, black burst, independent of the satellite antenna. The gateway is locked; CAM 2 is steady on program. Reference A is still drifting, but nothing strict depends on it.
items.caption: One change. The strict device now follows the one clock that didn't lose the sky.

items.label: **Fix it:** move the gateway to an independent reference — Tess's hands, your coaching.

items.alt: Tess at the rack, patch in hand; Maya beside her. The red alarm banner is gone.

bubbles.text: Gateway locks, CAM 2 stops tearing. If it doesn't, I'm wrong about the reference.
Then do it. One change. Watch.

lines.text: (Her hand is shaking. The change takes one second. The wait takes the rest of her life so far.)
(Maya doesn't touch anything. It's the hardest thing she does all night.)

items.title: Clocks that count atoms
items.body: In 1949 the U.S. National Bureau of Standards built a clock regulated by ammonia molecules; in 1955 Louis Essen and Jack Parry at Britain's National Physical Laboratory built the first accurate caesium clock. Satellite time — the time a studio reference locks to — descends from them.

items.alt: The monitor wall, calm. A status chip: gateway lock, nine minutes forty, zero losses. Tess breathes out.
items.caption: Ten minutes stable is a measurement. Thirty seconds stable is a hope.

lines.text: (off air, to the floor) Who's in master control tonight?
The trainee. And someone from a church.

items.prompt: 5:51. Nine minutes. The gateway has held for ten. The antenna is still dead. Call it.
items.happening: Gateway stable 10 min on house black.
items.risk: The valley's evening news — and whether Tess ever trusts herself.
timeout: Nobody calls it. At 5:59 the director asks the room, “Are we going?” and three people answer at once.
Somebody has to say go — calmly, with the fallback named.

hints.text: Who should be at the switcher every night after tonight?

options.label: Go to air on time: CAM 2 back in the plan, the two-camera fallback and a lower-third parked, Tess on the switcher
options.result: Tess nods. The director nods. Lena, at the door, doesn't say anything, which is how you know it's right.
options.consequence: A plan with a fallback, run by the person who'll run it every night.

options.label: Delay the news ten minutes to be sure
options.result: The water authority guest has to leave at 6:30.
options.consequence: You bought certainty with the story.
options.fail: You had ten stable minutes and a fallback. Delay costs the audience, not the risk.

options.label: Take the switcher yourself — Tess is too green
options.result: Tess steps back. She doesn't say anything.
options.consequence: The show goes fine. Tess learns she isn't trusted.
options.fail: She made the fix. Taking it away from her at the last minute teaches the opposite of what tonight was for.

options.label: Tell Lena it's fixed for good
options.consequence: The antenna is dead and Reference B still follows A.
options.fail: It's a workaround until facilities fix the antenna and B is made independent.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #32 · AVERY'S LENS  An alarm should say what to do  A warning that names the problem but not the next step leaves the person in front of it alone.  The wall said REFERENCE · SYNC ALARM. Cal's card said GATEWAY → HOUSE REF B. Only one of them helped Tess at 5:02.

items.alt: The news set, on air. Omar, the anchor, behind the desk. A lower third: Kestrel Valley News, live, 6:00 p.m.

bubbles.text: Good evening. The river is running high for October — and tonight we'll hear what that means for the valley.

items.caption: 6:00:00. On air. On time.

items.alt: Omar listens as a guest from the county water authority explains river gauges, a lower third behind them.

bubbles.text: The Old Mill gauge is three meters under flood stage. Nothing to worry about this week.

items.caption: Remember the Old Mill gauge.

items.title: Old Mill gauge — normal range
items.body: A laminated card the guest left on the desk: flood stage at the Old Mill bridge, the 1964 record line, and a phone number for the county emergency manager. Omar tucks it into the rundown binder. It will stay there until it matters.

items.alt: Master control: Tess on the headset, finger over the switcher, calling shots.
items.caption: CAM 2. Clean.

items.label: **Service Mode:** run the sixty minutes yourself. The story clock is compressed.

items.alt: Cal's fourteen warnings, printed and pinned to the master-control wall. Number three is circled in red. Maya points at it.
items.caption: Fourteen warnings. Tonight they bought one hour with number three. Nothing is crossed off yet — the antenna is still dead.

items.alt: The loading dock after the show. Lena and Maya in the drizzle.

bubbles.text: Two weeks. That's all I'm asking. Until I find someone.
Tonight, a trainee and a card on a door kept you on air. Start with them.

lines.text: The best engineer I ever had. He knows this station better than anyone alive.
Except maybe the man who wired it in 2004. An installer. Retired, mostly. Ray something.

items.alt: The next morning, the viewer inbox on a monitor: love the new anchor, but his lips don't match his words on the stream. Tess stares at it.
items.caption: Next: *Five Frames.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  When a picture fails “every few seconds,” look for the strictest device and the clock it follows. Read the reference before you reboot it. A backup that follows the main is not a backup. Write the fallback where the operator's eyes land — and let the operator make the change.

REFLECTION (optional)  · Cal wrote fourteen warnings and got one reply: “noted.” Is there a warning you've written that nobody answered — or one you've read and filed?  Boundary: this reflection doesn't fix the antenna.
